newsitem.title: UK: Commercial Union to pay $1.6m in US pollution case.
newsitem.headline: Commercial Union to pay $1.6m in US pollution case.

text.p: Commercial Union has been ordered to pay at least $1.6 million in costs and damages to a Pennsylvania manufacturer as a result of an environmental legal action.

Universal-Rundle Corporation of New Castle, Pennsylvania, said in a statement that a court in Camden County, PA, had ordered Commercial Union Insurance Co of Boston to reimburse it for approximately $660,000 lawyers' fees spent defending against an environmental lawsuit.
It added that the insurer would have to pay up to $1 million in costs which Universal-Rundle may spend in the future to remedy pollution.
Commercial Union of Boston is a US unit of UK insurance giant Commercial Union. A spokesperson for the company was not immediately available for comment.
After a six-day bench trial, Judge E. Stevenson Fluharty found that Commercial Union had a "preconceived intent to deny the claim", and that its position lacked merit, Universal-Rundle said.
The court also awarded Universal-Rundle the lawyers' fees spent in pursuing Commercial Union to enforce insurance coverage, according to the statement.

Universal-Rundle had owned and operated a bathtub factory in Pennsauken, New Jersey from approximately 1935 to 1973. During that time, Universal-Rundle deposited large quantities of burnt foundry sand, ash and porcelain enamel chips in a marsh behind the factory. Some of the enamel chips contained lead.

In 1989, the groundwater around the site was found to be contaminated by lead and other substances. Vineland Construction Co., which had purchased the factory from Universal-Rundle in 1973, blamed Universal-Rundle for causing the contamination.

Commercial Union had sold comprehensive general liability insurance to Universal-Rundle, but refused to cover the claim, the manufacturers lawyers said. Commercial Union argued that Universal-Rundle had intentionally harmed the environment, forfeiting insurance coverage.

"The insurance industry has taken a very hard line on these environmental insurance coverage cases," said Carl A. Salisbury of East Hanover, New Jersey, one of the lawyers who represented Universal-Rundle.
"They like to take the premiums, but they hate to pay the claims," he added.
According to Salisbury, insurance companies try to apply 1990s environmental standards to 1960s conduct, and then argue that the policyholder "should have known" it was causing environmental damage.

"Unfortunately for companies like Commercial Union, many courts are able to recognise that 'should have known' means negligence, not intentional harm. And negligence is what insurance is for," added Salisbury's partner, Eugene Killian, Jr.
